newsitem.title: USA: Goldman analyst sees higher commodities prices.
newsitem.headline: Goldman analyst sees higher commodities prices.

text.p: Steve Strongin, director of commodities research at Goldman Sachs & Co, expects commodities prices to rise, Barron's financial weekly quoted him as saying.
"Well, I think, from a return standpoint, they are really headed up," he told the paper in an interview, answering a question on the direction of commodities prices.
Energy and agriculture commodities have been strong in the current economic cycle, while metals have been weaker, Strongin, the keeper of the Goldman Sachs Commodities Index, told the paper.
Strongin sees higher prices for good quality crude oils and less upward pressure on lower grade crude oils, partly because of higher demands for diesel fuel, Barron's said.

Oil prices should stabilize a little bit above $21 a barrel as planned maintenance schedules end, Strongin said. Prices are expected to trade within $2 of that level as demand growth continues, he told the paper.
On Friday, June crude closed at $19.99 a barrel.
Asian demand could swing prices for oil, with a slowdown dropping oil prices and acceleration of those economies pushing prices as high as $26 or $27 a barrel, Strongin said.

Regarding agricultural products, feed grains are now in a shortage and soybeans will have record low inventories this year, Strongin said. The low inventories will lead to greater plantings of soybeans, but that could generate a shortage in corn or wheat, or both, Strongin said.
Strongin told Barron's that the recent increases of industrial metals prices is based on an optimism about European and Japanese growth.
"If both of them (the economies) grow above trend, which is not the current forecast, that could lead to inflation," Strongin told Barron's adding that the situation is not an "immediate concern."
